case_name: Damji Valji Shah And Another v Life Insurance Corporation Of India & Ors.

statutes.act: Provided That No Civil Court Would Have Jurisdiction To Entertain Or Adjudicate Upon Any Matter Which A Tribunal Was Empowered To Decide Or Determine Under The Act
Inter Alia Provided That Nothing Contained In The Act

facts: The company was a composite insurer, i.e., an insurer who carried on in addition to life insurance business other classes of-insurance business.
On July 1, 1956, the LIC Act came into force and the Corporation was established on September 1, 1956, which was the 'appointed day' according to s. 2(1) of that Act.
The company had to keep separate accounts of all receipts and payments in respect of each class of insurance business, in view of s. 10(1) of the Insurance Act.

By resolution dated December 18, 1948, Rs. 1,10,000/- were transferred from the General Department to the Life Department as advance to the Life Department Revenue Account for being added to the Life Fund.
The Profit & Loss Appropriation Account for the year 1949 shows that Rs. 60,000/- out of this amount was written off as the company had made profits.
Rs. 32,000/- were again similarly transferred to the Life Fund from the General Department with retrospective effect from December 31, 1952 in order to strengthen the position of the Life Fund.

The second actuarial valuation report for the period 1949-52, dated September 9, 1953, showed that the policy liability amounted to Rs. 15,33,068, that the Life Fund stood at Rs. 15,35,890/- and that thus the Life Fund exceeded the net liability by Rs. 2,822/-.
The resolution of January 6, 1956 was confirmed by the Board of Directors at its meeting dated February 6, 1956.
On January 19, 1956, the Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1956 was promulgated by the President and came into force from that day which was called the 'appointed day'.
The LIC Act came into force on July 1, 1956 and the Corporation was established on September 1, 1956.
The transfer and vesting in the Corporation of all the assets and liabilities pertaining to the life insurance business took place in view of s. 7 of that Act.
issues: What is the nature of the transaction involving the transfer of Rs. 82,000/- from the Life Fund to the General Department?
Is the resolution of January 6, 1956 valid and binding on the parties concerned?
Can the Corporation apply for relief under s. 15 of the LIC Act in respect of this transaction?
petitioner_arguments: The transfer of Rs. 82,000/- from the Life Fund to the General Department was illegal.
The resolution of January 6, 1956 was not valid and binding on the parties concerned.
The Corporation can apply for relief under s. 15 of the LIC Act in respect of this transaction.
respondent_arguments: The transfer of Rs. 82,000/- from the Life Fund to the General Department was legal and valid.
The resolution of January 6, 1956 was valid and binding on the parties concerned.
The Corporation cannot apply for relief under s. 15 of the LIC Act in respect of this transaction.
court_reasoning: The Court held that the transfer of Rs. 82,000/- from the Life Fund to the General Department was illegal and invalid.
The resolution of January 6, 1956 was not valid and binding on the parties concerned.
The Corporation can apply for relief under s. 15 of the LIC Act in respect of this transaction.
holding: The Court ordered that the sum of Rs. 82,000/- be paid to the Corporation jointly and severally by the directors of the Vishwabharti Insurance Company.
